summary: Explains the general ways other protocols and applications can use Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) to learn quickly that a path has failed. It sets out how a client protocol, such as a routing protocol, can rely on BFD for fast failure detection. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: BFD is a small protocol that checks whether a path is still alive by sending its own packets back and forth. This document says how the rest of the system should use it: BFD reports that a path failed, and each client reacts with the failure handling it already has, such as withdrawing an adjacency. BFD never runs the client itself.

subtitle: How routing protocols and other network functions should use BFD's fast failure signal without letting it run their lives.

tldr.problem: Many network functions need to learn quickly that a path has failed, but their own liveness checks are too slow, unsuitable or missing. Writing a separate BFD document for each one would take a long series of short documents.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5882 describes in general terms how a client such as a routing protocol supplies session parameters to BFD, receives session state back, and reacts using its own existing mechanisms. BFD acts only as an advisory service.
tldr.outcome: Because clients react with mechanisms they already have, BFD use has essentially no interoperability issues, and one system can use BFD even if its neighbor does not.

facts.label: BFD sessions per data protocol path

today: RFC 5882 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2010, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the general companion to the BFD protocol in RFC 5880.

sections.title: Why a Generic Description
sections.content:
The Bidirectional Forwarding Detection protocol provides a liveness detection mechanism that other network components can use when their own liveness mechanisms are too slow, inappropriate or nonexistent. Other documents detail the use of BFD with specific encapsulations, for single-hop, multihop and MPLS paths.

As the usefulness of BFD became clear, there were calls to specify BFD interactions with a growing list of network functions. Rather than producing a long series of short documents on the application of BFD, the document says it seemed worthwhile to describe the interactions between BFD and other network functions, which it calls BFD clients, in a broad way. This document describes the generic application of BFD, and gives specific protocol applications for illustrative purposes.
sections.plainLanguage: BFD was specified for particular encapsulations first. This document fills the gap in between, so that each new protocol does not need its own short document explaining how to react to a BFD failure.

sections.title: What BFD Provides
sections.content:
The BFD specification defines a protocol with simple and specific semantics. Its sole purpose is to verify connectivity between a pair of systems for a particular data protocol across a path, which may be of any technology, length or OSI layer. How promptly a path failure is detected can be controlled by trading off protocol overhead and system load against detection times.

BFD is not intended to provide control protocol liveness information directly, because those protocols have their own means and vagaries. Control protocols can use the services provided by BFD to inform their operation, and BFD can be viewed as a service provided by the layer in which it is running.

The service interface is straightforward. The application supplies the session parameters, namely the neighbor address, the time parameters and the protocol options, and BFD provides the session state, of which the most interesting transitions are to and from the Up state. The application is expected to bootstrap the BFD session, because BFD has no discovery mechanism.

An implementation SHOULD establish only a single BFD session per data protocol path, regardless of how many applications want to use it, because multiple sessions to the same endpoints add nothing. If several applications ask for different session parameters, resolving the conflict is a local matter. BFD notifies all applications bound to a session when the session state changes.

BFD should be viewed as having an advisory role towards the protocols or other network functions it interacts with, which then use their own mechanisms to make any state transitions. The interaction is at arm's length, which keeps things simple and decoupled. In particular, BFD explicitly does not carry application-specific information, partly for architectural reasons and partly because BFD may have unpredictable latency and so makes a poor transport mechanism.

Because BFD acts in an advisory manner and the clients use their existing mechanisms to react to BFD events, the interaction between BFD and its clients has essentially no interoperability issues. BFD may even interact with only one of a pair of systems for a particular client application without any ill effect.
sections.plainLanguage: BFD answers one question: is this path still working? The client sets the session up, gives BFD the address and the timers, and then gets told when the state changes. BFD carries no information of its own for the client and makes no decisions for it.

sections.title: Session State, Hysteresis and AdminDown
sections.content:
The interaction between a BFD session and its client applications is for the most part an implementation issue outside the scope of this specification, but the document describes mechanisms implementers may use to promote full-featured implementations. One way of modelling the interaction is to create an adaptation layer between the BFD state machine and the client applications that is aware of both the internals of the BFD implementation and the requirements of the clients.

On session state hysteresis, a BFD session can be tightly coupled to its clients, so that any transition out of the Up state causes failure signalling to the clients. But implementers may choose to hide rapid Up, Down, Up transitions from their clients, which is useful for supporting process restarts without needing complex protocol mechanisms. A system MAY therefore choose not to notify clients if a session goes from Up to Down and back to Up within a reasonable period, whose length is outside the scope of the specification. If the session does not return to Up within that time frame, the clients SHOULD be notified that a session failure has occurred.

The AdminDown mechanism in BFD is intended to signal that the session is being taken down for administrative purposes and that the session state is not indicative of the liveness of the data path. A system SHOULD NOT indicate a connectivity failure to a client if the local or the remote session state transitions to AdminDown, as long as that client has independent means of liveness detection, typically a control protocol. If a client has no independent means of liveness detection, a system SHOULD indicate a connectivity failure to it and assume the semantics of the Down state, because otherwise the client cannot determine whether the path is viable and unfortunate results may occur.

It is useful to configure a BFD session between a pair of systems without affecting the state of the clients associated with it, and equally useful for BFD state to be reestablished without perturbing those clients when all BFD state is lost, as in a process restart. The BFD state machine transitions that occur while a session is brought up in such situations SHOULD NOT cause a connectivity failure notification to the clients. A client that is capable of establishing its state prior to the configuration or restarting of a BFD session MAY do so if appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: Three situations need care. A session that flops up and down again in a moment is often not worth telling the client about. A session that was shut down on purpose says nothing about the path, so it should not look like a failure. And setting a session up, or setting it up again after a restart, should not disturb the client either.

sections.title: How Control Protocols React
sections.content:
The most common clients of BFD are control protocols such as routing protocols. The object of the interaction is to advise the control protocol of the connectivity of the data protocol, so that a connectivity failure triggers rerouting around the failed path more quickly than the native detection mechanisms of the control protocol would.

On adjacency establishment, if the session state on either the local or the remote system is AdminDown, BFD has been administratively disabled and the establishment of a control protocol adjacency MUST be allowed. BFD sessions are typically bootstrapped by the control protocol, using the discovery or configuration mechanism that the control protocol uses to find neighbours. It is possible for the network to be in a state where the control protocol could come up but the BFD session cannot be established, and data cannot be forwarded. To avoid that, the establishment of control protocol adjacencies SHOULD be blocked if both systems are willing to establish a BFD session but a BFD session cannot be established. One way of determining that both systems are willing is for the control protocol to signal it explicitly; if there is no explicit signalling, willingness may be determined by means outside the scope of the specification. If it is believed that the neighbouring system does not support BFD, the establishment of a control protocol adjacency SHOULD NOT be blocked.

The setting of BFD's timing parameters and modes is not subject to standardization, and all protocols sharing a session use the same parameters. It is generally useful to choose the parameters giving the shortest detection time, because a client that wants longer detection times can apply hysteresis to the notifications from BFD.

On reacting to state changes, if a session goes from Up to AdminDown, or from Up to Down because the remote system says the session is in AdminDown, clients SHOULD NOT take any control protocol action. For other transitions from Up to Down, the mechanism depends on the protocol. A control protocol tightly bound to a single failing data protocol SHOULD act to ensure that data traffic is no longer directed to the failing path. This should not be read as BFD replacing the control protocol liveness mechanism, because the control protocol may rely on mechanisms that BFD does not verify, such as multicast, so BFD most likely cannot detect all failures that would affect it. A control protocol MAY however use BFD session state to detect an impending failure more rapidly, particularly when it operates in band over the data protocol. When a session goes from Up to Down, action SHOULD be taken in the control protocol to signal the lack of connectivity for the path over which BFD is running. If the control protocol has an explicit mechanism for announcing path state, that mechanism SHOULD be used rather than affecting the connectivity of the control protocol itself, particularly when it operates out of band. If there is no such mechanism, a control protocol timeout SHOULD be emulated for the associated neighbour.

Where a control protocol carries several data protocols, the mechanism differs. With a shared topology, if one of the data protocols fails, the path has to be considered failed for all of them, because otherwise the control protocol cannot turn away the traffic of the failed data protocol and that traffic would be black-holed indefinitely. Action SHOULD then be taken to signal the lack of connectivity for the path in the topology corresponding to the BFD session, and if it cannot be signalled otherwise a control protocol timeout SHOULD be emulated. With individual routing topologies for each data protocol, only the failed data protocol needs to be rerouted, and this can generally be done without affecting the connectivity of the other topologies.

Graceful Restart mechanisms, supported by IS-IS, OSPF and BGP, let a control protocol restart without perturbing network connectivity state, and are predicated on a separate forwarding plane that does not necessarily share fate with the control plane. BFD implementations announce through the Control Plane Independent, or C, bit whether BFD shares fate with the control plane, and this is used to decide what to do with Graceful Restart. If BFD does not share fate with the control plane on either system, a BFD session failure means data can no longer be forwarded, so any Graceful Restart in progress SHOULD be aborted to avoid black holes and a topology change SHOULD be signalled. If BFD shares fate with the control plane on either system, a session failure cannot be disentangled from other events in the control plane, and in many cases the session will fail as a side effect of the restart, so it is best to avoid aborting a Graceful Restart if possible, at the risk that a simultaneous failure of the forwarding plane will not be detected.

Where a control protocol can signal a planned restart in advance, a BFD session failure during the restart SHOULD NOT abort it and SHOULD NOT result in a topology change being signalled. Where it cannot, the restarted system depends on the recently restarted system to signal the Graceful Restart before the adjacency timeout, and in most cases the BFD session will time out first, in which case a topology change SHOULD be signalled. An implementation MAY instead adjust the BFD session timing parameters before restarting so that the detection time in each direction is longer than the restart period of the control protocol, and the restarting system SHOULD NOT send any BFD control packets until there is a high likelihood that its neighbours know a Graceful Restart is taking place, because the first BFD control packet will cause the session to fail.

When several control protocols want BFD sessions with the same remote system for the same data protocol, all MUST share a single BFD session. Where hierarchical or dependent layers of control protocols are in use, such as OSPF and IBGP, it may not be useful for more than one of them to interact with BFD, because IBGP depends on OSPF for its routing information, so the faster failure detection relayed to IBGP may actually be detrimental. It is generally best for the protocol at the lowest point in the hierarchy to interact with BFD and then use the existing interactions between the control protocols to effect the necessary changes, which gives the fastest failure detection and recovery.
sections.plainLanguage: The client reacts with the failure handling it already has: drop the adjacency, or pretend the neighbour timed out. BFD does not do the reacting, and it does not need both ends to take part. When a protocol restarts on purpose, BFD is told whether it survives that restart, and the two signals are reconciled so a planned restart is not mistaken for a failure.

sections.title: Non-Protocol Functions and Data Protocol Demultiplexing
sections.content:
BFD session status may be used to affect other system functions that are not protocol based, for example static routes. If the path to a remote system fails, it may be desirable to avoid passing traffic to that remote system, so the local system may take internal measures such as withdrawing a static route and withdrawing that route from the routing protocols. If it is known or presumed that the remote system is BFD capable and the session is not in the Up state, appropriate action SHOULD be taken. If it is known or presumed that the remote system does not support BFD, action such as withdrawing a static route SHOULD NOT be taken. Bootstrapping the session in this non-protocol case is likely to come from configuration information, and there is no need to exchange endpoints or discriminator values by any mechanism other than configuration, since the endpoints must be known and configured by the same means.

BFD is intended to protect a single data protocol and is encapsulated within that protocol. A pair of systems may have multiple BFD sessions over the same topology if they support different protocols. For example, if two systems run IPv4 and IPv6 across the same link, these are considered two separate paths and require two separate BFD sessions. The same technique is used for more fine-grained paths: if several differentiated services are operated over IPv4, an independent BFD session may be run for each service level. The BFD control packets must be marked in the same way as the data packets, partly to ensure as much fate sharing as possible between BFD and the data traffic, and also to demultiplex the initial packet if the discriminator values have not been exchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: Static routes can follow BFD too, but only where the neighbour is known to run BFD, because otherwise a static route would be withdrawn for no reason. Each data protocol needs its own session, and the BFD packets must be marked like the data they protect.

sections.title: Running BFD Over Aggregated Links
sections.content:
A number of technologies aggregate several parallel links at layer N-1 and treat them as a single link at layer N. BFD may be used in several ways to protect the path at layer N, and the exact mechanism is outside the scope of this specification, but the document gives examples of possible deployment scenarios and says others are possible and not precluded.

The simplest approach is complete decoupling: run BFD over the layer N path with no interaction with the layer N-1 mechanism, which assumes that mechanism will deal with connectivity issues in the individual layer N-1 links. BFD then declares a failure in the layer N path only when the session times out. This works whether or not the layer N-1 neighbour is the same as the layer N neighbour.

A slightly more intelligent approach is to use layer N-1 hints, where the layer N-1 mechanism informs the layer N BFD when the aggregated link is no longer viable. The session then detects the failure more rapidly, because it need not wait to time out, which is analogous to triggering a session failure based on a hardware-detected failure of a single link. This also works whether or not the two neighbours are the same.

Aggregating BFD sessions is a third approach: run BFD on each layer N-1 link and aggregate the state of the several sessions into a single indication to the layer N clients. The advantage is that it does not depend on the layer N-1 technology, but it only works if the layer N neighbour is the same as the layer N-1 neighbour, that is, a single hop at layer N-1.

Combinations may be useful. For example, if the layer N neighbour is not directly connected at layer N-1, a system might run a BFD session across each layer N-1 link to the immediate layer N-1 neighbour and then run another BFD session to the layer N neighbour, using the aggregate state of the layer N-1 sessions to trigger a layer N session failure.
sections.plainLanguage: Where several links are bundled into one, BFD can be run over the bundle, told by the bundling layer when the bundle breaks, or run on each link and the results combined. The last option needs both ends to be the same neighbour, so it does not work everywhere.

sections.title: Examples with Specific Protocols
sections.content:
The document says there are no interoperability concerns regarding interactions between BFD and control protocols, but that there is enough concern and confusion in the area to be worth giving examples with specific protocols. Since the interactions do not affect interoperability, these examples are non-normative.

OSPFv2, OSPFv3 and IS-IS all suffer from an architectural limitation: their Hello protocols are limited in the granularity of their failure detection times, with a minimum detection time of two seconds for OSPF and one second for IS-IS. BFD may be used to achieve arbitrarily small detection times for these protocols by supplementing the Hello protocols used in each case. The most obvious choice for triggering BFD session establishment is the discovery mechanism inherent in the Hello protocols in OSPF and IS-IS, and any BFD sessions established to support OSPF and IS-IS across a single IP hop must operate in accordance with the single-hop BFD specification.

Because OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 carry routing information for a single data protocol, IPv4 and IPv6 respectively, a topology change after a BFD session failure should be signalled by tearing down the corresponding OSPF neighbour. IS-IS may support one data protocol or several. IS-IS specifies a common topology for multiple data protocols, with work under way to support multiple topologies. If multiple topologies are used, the topology-specific path associated with a failing BFD session should no longer be advertised in IS-IS label switched paths to signal a lack of connectivity; otherwise a failing session should be signalled by simulating an IS-IS adjacency failure. OSPF has a planned restart signalling mechanism and IS-IS does not, so the appropriate mechanisms apply to each.

If BFD is used for failure detection of OSPF virtual links, the multihop BFD mechanism MUST be used, because virtual links may traverse an arbitrary number of hops, and BFD authentication SHOULD be used and is strongly encouraged.

For BGP, BFD may be useful with external sessions in order to trigger topology changes more rapidly in the face of a path failure. As with the general rules, it is generally unwise for IBGP sessions to interact with BFD if the underlying IGP is already doing so. An external session advised by BFD may establish either a one-hop or a multihop session depending on whether the neighbour is immediately adjacent, and the session should be established to the BGP neighbour rather than to any other next hop advertised in BGP. BFD authentication SHOULD be used and is strongly encouraged. If Graceful Restart is not taking place on an external session and the BFD session fails, the session should be torn down; if it is taking place, the general procedures apply, and because BGP Graceful Restart does not signal planned restarts, the rules for control protocols without planned restart signalling apply.

RIP is somewhat unique, because at least as specified the neighbour adjacency state is not stored per se: installed routes contain a next hop address, which in most cases is the address of the advertising neighbour but may not be. When the BFD session associated with a neighbour fails, an expiration of the timeout timer for each route installed from that neighbour, for which the neighbour is the next hop, should be simulated. If a route is received from that neighbour with a next hop address that is not the neighbour's own address, the route will linger until it naturally times out after 180 seconds, unless the implementation keeps track of all routes received from each neighbour, in which case all of the routes from that neighbour should be timed out regardless of the next hop, avoiding the lingering route problem.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show what this means in practice. A routing protocol with a slow Hello timer can use BFD for a much faster failure signal, and then reacts by dropping the adjacency as if the neighbour had timed out. RIP is the awkward case, because it keeps no adjacency state, so the routes themselves have to be timed out.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document states that this specification raises no additional security issues beyond those of the specifications referred to in the list of normative references.

The document does add a note in its discussion of specific protocols that BFD authentication SHOULD be used for OSPF virtual links and for external BGP sessions, and is strongly encouraged. Because BFD is advisory, it also observes that the interaction between BFD and other protocols is very loosely coupled: the actions taken are based on existing mechanisms in those protocols, so interoperability problems are very unlikely unless BFD is applied in contradictory ways, such as a BFD session failure causing one implementation to go down and another to come up. BFD may be advising one system for a particular control function but not the other, and the only impact of this would be potentially asymmetric control protocol failure detection.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds no new security problems of its own. It does recommend turning on BFD authentication where it matters, and it notes that because BFD only advises, a mismatched pair of systems can end up disagreeing about whether a path is up.

viz.caption: THE BFD SESSION STATES THAT CLIENTS REACT TO
WHAT THE CLIENT SHOULD DO IN EACH CASE

items.title: Up to Down
items.text: The client acts: drop the adjacency or emulate a protocol timeout.

items.title: Up to AdminDown
items.text: No control protocol action, unless the client has no other way to detect liveness.

items.title: Rapid Up, Down, Up
items.text: The transition may be hidden from the client, as in a process restart.

items.title: Session set up or restarted
items.text: The client should not be told the path failed.

viz.caption: THE THREE WAYS TO PROTECT AN AGGREGATED LINK WITH BFD

cells: Run BFD over the layer N path only
Nothing from the layer N-1 mechanism
The bundling layer tells the session the link is dead
The layer N-1 mechanism to report it
Run BFD on each layer N-1 link and combine the results
The layer N and layer N-1 neighbours to be the same
